_note: DECLARED / INDUCED learning outcomes for the book. Each outcome has a PRIMARY unit (where it is chiefly taught — drives coverage) and optional secondary_units (elaborative: reinforce/extend/apply). Keys are outline unit ids (section_id | chapter-slug | part-N | book). Hand-authored SOURCE — this file IS edited by hand; outcomes.json + outcomes-draft.md are generated from it. Each declaration: {granularity (of the primary), primary_unit, secondary_units?, verb (from BLOOM_VERBS), obj, statement?, provenance, anchor?, gap_note?}. provenance is 'derived' (grounded in what the primary unit actually teaches — cite the grounding prose in anchor), 'declared' (thin prose roughly supports it), or 'gap-recommended' (content the unit ought to deliver but does not yet — cite gap_note). COVERAGE: primary drives it; an elaborative-only unit is still a gap. Do NOT manufacture aspirational outcomes to fill slots. See book-models/DESIGN.md 2.6.

declarations.obj: one-shot scripting from supervised autonomy
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can distinguish one-shot scripting from supervised autonomy and name what each supplies to the agent.
declarations.anchor: point: not-every-task-deserves-the-full-apparatus-of-governed-autonomy / two-things-shorten-the-leash-reasoning-burden-and-assurance-need (re-homed to 'Size Work to Reasoning and Assurance' in 4.1 the MAGE Workflow; one-shot-scripting vs supervised-autonomy).

declarations.obj: why an agent needs a model of how to build the thing, not just a picture of it
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why an agent, like a 3D printer, needs the detailed build instructions and not merely a picture of the desired result.
declarations.anchor: point: modeling-and-alignment-supply-the-instruction-package (The Printer, 'The Engineering Object' — intent is not fabrication instructions; a photograph does not specify the build).

declarations.obj: the posture that when an agent produces the wrong thing, the first suspect is the instructions
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can adopt the posture that an agent is a printer, not a stapler — so when it produces the wrong thing, the first suspect is the instructions, and the models can build anything one can explain.

declarations.obj: a governed environment in which a fleet of coding agents does useful engineering work at bounded risk
declarations.statement: After the book, the reader can design a governed engineering environment in which a fleet of coding agents produces correct work at bounded risk — choosing the right mechanism, the right model, and the right transformation for each failure class.
declarations.anchor: Preface 'Who this book is for': recognize when an engineering problem is being paid for repeatedly in reconstruction or human judgment; decide whether a better representation, stronger enforcement, or both would retire that cost; and design mechanisms suited to your own system rather than copying another organization's process.

declarations.obj: a constraint from a sensor and a soft mechanism from a hard one
declarations.statement: After the book, the reader can situate any governance move on the two thesis axes — constraint-vs-sensor and soft-vs-hard — and reach for the one the failure calls for.
declarations.anchor: The two book-thesis axes (Alignment: constraint/sensor; soft/hard) run through Part 2 (constraints-and-sensors) and Part 4 (guidance-or-enforcement, in the MAGE Workflow chapter — re-homed in round-6).

declarations.obj: a system as a small set of structured, drift-checked 4+1 views
declarations.statement: After the book, the reader can model a system as structured, drift-checked views an agent reasons through, rather than leaving the structure in a human's head.
declarations.anchor: The Modeling Principle, developed across Part 3 (the executable 4+1 zoo).

declarations.obj: which tasks warrant the book's machinery, given that implementation is abundant and judgment scarce, and how to read an agent as a loop conditioned by the model you give it
declarations.statement: After this Part, the reader can judge which engineering tasks warrant the book's machinery — grounded in the founding premise that implementation has become abundant, so judgment is the scarce resource — and read an agent as a loop whose behavior you condition by handing it a model of its world.
declarations.anchor: 1.1 'Not every programming task needs the machinery this book describes' + the founding premise (commodity intelligence → judgment is the scarce resource) + 1.3 'an agent runs in a loop … give it a model of the world'.

declarations.obj: a system as the small set of models it needs — chosen from five classes of model (behavioral, structural, decision, measurement, documentation), each kept honest by a drift check
declarations.statement: After this Part, the reader can model a system as the small set of models it needs, choosing from five classes of model — behavioral, structural, decision, measurement, and documentation — rather than completing a fixed taxonomy, each a structured model kept honest by a drift check, and can join them around a scenario.
declarations.anchor: Modeling moves through five classes of model across eight chapters (context, engineering model, executable models, views as projections, structure, behavior and execution, measurement and evidence, and the scenario join), each kept honest by a drift check.

declarations.obj: the governed environment — its layers, its ex-ante and ex-post mechanisms, its lifecycles, and its metrics
declarations.statement: After this Part, the reader can construct a governed engineering environment: place a control at the right layer of the agent stack, split ex-ante from ex-post, write lifecycles and runbooks, and measure one level deeper.
declarations.anchor: Alignment chapter arc: agent-stack -> semantic-gap -> governed-environment (ex-ante/ex-post) -> lifecycles/runbooks -> metrics -> when-guardrails-collide.

declarations.obj: the method to a real codebase — running the MAGE workflow loop, inducing models from brownfield code, wielding the skills, holding the result with generative validation, and converting recurring failures into mechanisms
declarations.statement: After this Part, the reader can put the method to work: run the MAGE workflow loop, induce models from an existing codebase, deploy the self-operate / self-govern / self-communicate skills, hold the result with generative validation, and convert a recurring failure into a durable mechanism.
declarations.anchor: The MAGE Method chapter arc: the-mage-workflow -> brownfield -> validating-change -> the-skills (governance-conversion + field-guide dissolved into 4.1 + the 4.4 synthesis close in round-6).

declarations.obj: the method's evolution through a real accessibility-remediation system
declarations.statement: After this Part, the reader can trace how the method grew from a single reviewer to a multi-agent engineering organization in one real system, and relate each governance move to the problem that forced it.
declarations.anchor: The Evidence is the ADA/DocAble case study: context -> timeline/work -> built-system -> road-to-MAGE (role progression).

declarations.obj: what the method changes for how software engineering is measured, staffed, and taught
declarations.statement: After this Part, the reader can evaluate the method's implications for the discipline — where the judgment moved, what stays human, and where models become a common language of mature engineering.

declarations.obj: when an open-ended task needs governance and who is accountable when an agent gets it wrong
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can judge whether a task is open-ended enough to need the book's machinery, and reason about accountability when an agent produces a wrong result.

declarations.obj: the convert-a-failure-into-a-mechanism move on two real incidents, using DocAble as the grounding case
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can recognize the convert-a-failure-into-a-mechanism move on two real incidents, using DocAble — what it does and how its six parts fit — as the grounding case.

declarations.obj: the two engineering problems from the two properties of the agentic substrate
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can name the two properties of the agentic substrate — a finite, reconstructed reasoning state that meets a scale-driven locality problem, and probabilistic work that cannot certify itself but crosses an interposable, observable harness — and derive the two engineering problems, representation and enforcement, that follow, without treating either as a prerequisite of the other.

declarations.obj: the two engineering problems and why MAGE develops Modeling first as a methodological choice
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain the two engineering problems — representation (Problem A, Part II) and enforcement (Problem B, Part III) — and why they are related but independent, so MAGE develops Modeling first as a methodological choice rather than a logical prerequisite of Alignment.

declarations.obj: guidance from authority and place a mechanism at the intervention boundary where the relevant obligation is legible
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can distinguish guidance from authority, place a mechanism at the intervention boundary where the relevant obligation is legible, and recognize that where a mechanism acts and how much authority it carries are separate decisions.

declarations.obj: why agreement is not correctness and place a mechanism at the earliest boundary where the obligation is legible and enforceable
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain why agreement is not correctness — authority needs an obligation independent of the work being judged — and place a mechanism at the earliest boundary where that obligation is legible and enforceable.

declarations.obj: ex-ante obligations from ex-post ones and convert a recurring failure into the durable structure it was missing as engineering capital
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can split ex-ante obligations from ex-post ones, convert a recurring failure into the durable structure it was missing — a model, invariant, sensor, validator, or authority — as engineering capital, and place any obligation among residual, judgment-required, observed-only, or governed.

declarations.obj: a lifecycle and a runbook that splits the deterministic from the judgment
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can author a lifecycle and its runbook, giving the deterministic parts a tight algorithm and the judgment parts the roughest one that still fits.
declarations.anchor: point: a-lifecycle-is-the-healthy-path-then-a-failure-map / type-each-runbook-step-execute-delegate-escalate (Operating MAGE, ch. 4.4 — lifecycles + externalized-judgment runbooks).

declarations.obj: a metric that measures one level deeper than the surface number
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can design a metric that measures one level deeper — turning a number that reports into one that drives a decision — and place it on the hard-to-soft spectrum, feeding a hard number into a structured model the metric tool then consumes.
declarations.anchor: point: ousterhouts-rule-measure-one-level-deeper / some-evidence-is-mechanically-decidable-other-evidence-is-judgment-laden (Operating MAGE, ch. 4.4 — 'Measure the State That Matters' + its hard/soft examples).

declarations.obj: accumulated control machinery through three views — catalogue, interaction graph, and coverage — and grow, reconcile, and retire controls so the machinery stays coherent
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can govern accumulated control machinery through three views — a catalogue of what exists, an interaction graph of what collides over a shared resource, and a coverage relation of obligations against mechanisms — and grow, reconcile, and retire controls so the machinery stays coherent.

declarations.obj: why a fleet pays for free the modeling expense that once buried MBSE
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain why the standing cost that kept explicit models secondary in code-centric practice is one an agent fleet now absorbs, so modeling becomes an economical first move.
declarations.anchor: Part-II intro: maintaining another representation carried a standing cost; commodity intelligence changes that economics.

declarations.obj: a service-flow model and the domain registries it rests on
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model the logical view as a structured service-flow model backed by frozen domain registries.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'service-flow-model' + 'domain-registries'; ts: 'The typed source-of-truth for a service-oriented architecture'.

declarations.obj: the concurrency of a system with a synchronization model and formal invariant verification
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model the process view — cataloging every lock in a synchronization model and backing its invariants with formal verification.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'formal-invariant-verification' + 'synchronization-model' (ts: 'A typed registry that models the system's synchronization behavior — every OS-level lock').

declarations.obj: a codebase's zones with a component & zone model and a rule-metadata registry
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model the development view — every component's zone and the governance rules that ride it — as typed registries.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'component-zone-model' + 'rule-metadata-registry'; ts: 'A typed catalog of every component's code zone'.

declarations.obj: where a system runs with a deployment-topology model and an invariant-DAG execution policy
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model the physical view — deployment topology and a typed deploy DAG — and name the one honest gap in the cost view.

declarations.obj: what the running system promises and the record it must leave behind
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can model an operating envelope — naming measured quantities and the bounds that drive admission or merely report — and derive an audit-grade changelog from a provenance record the code writes as it acts.

declarations.obj: user and developer journeys to test placement through a chain of structured models
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can map journeys to the environment tier that tests them, joining user-journey, orchestration, criticality, and coverage models.

declarations.obj: three approaches to inducing a model from existing code
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can apply top-down, bottom-up, and lint-cover-then-induce approaches to bring a brownfield codebase under a model.

declarations.obj: a recurring procedure as engineering capital, distinguishing the knowledge a skill preserves from the authority only surrounding machinery carries
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can package a recurring procedure as a skill — a base model, orthogonal models, and a decision procedure — recognize that packaging preserves knowledge capital but does not by itself grant authority, and treat the three shipped skills as instances of one portable architecture rather than as required parts of MAGE.

declarations.obj: each task to a leap the fleet can make and evaluate — big enough to use the model's power, small enough to check the result
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can size each task to a leap the fleet can make and evaluate, and tell a right-sized leap from a wrong-shaped one.
declarations.anchor: Section title 'task-sizing' (the sizing habit re-homed from Part I) — the modest task-sizing framing plus the DocAble bounded-typed-edits example.

declarations.obj: how engineering failures leave behind several FORMS of durable capital — representation, decision rule, deterministic check, behavioral model, derived provenance, provisional measurement — some granted authority and some deliberately not, reading the case as evidence of mechanism and sequence rather than prevalence
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can trace how a failure becomes durable engineering capital (or deliberately remains provisional), distinguish the ex-post and ex-ante paths, and state what a single longitudinal case can and cannot establish.
declarations.anchor: The eight episode sections under the standardized template ('The instruction satisfied to the letter' through 'Measurement: the story that stops before the gate', 5.4.1-5.4.8), the ex-ante confirmation 'Not every useful structure has an incident arc' (5.4.9), and the bounded epistemic close 'What this case supports' (5.4.10) in the chapter with identity label 'failures'.

declarations.obj: the evidence system for a change — choosing the model-surface each validation technique turns into an oracle
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can design the evidence system for a change: choose the model-surface that becomes the oracle, and select among generative-validation techniques by the specification each one attacks rather than by a maturity ladder.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'the-model-as-oracle', 'choosing-the-validation-technique' (with property-based-testing / fuzzing / when-to-reach-for-which under it), 'coverage-did-the-validation-explore-the-claim', 'deterministic-admission', 'why-this-matters-in-the-agentic-era' (round-8 W1 4.3.1–4.3.6 reorg).

declarations.obj: why document accessibility is a hard, high-burden problem worth this machinery
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain the accessibility problem the case-study system solves and why a document is not just a file.

declarations.obj: the project's stages to the kinds of work each demanded and the velocity each produced
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can map the case-study project's stages to the kinds of work each demanded and the velocity each produced.

declarations.obj: how the built system forced the method out of it — the delegation staircase from solo co-coder to architect, each rung safe only because the step below minted the control it needed
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can trace the delegation staircase — co-coder, QA, review lead, tech lead, architect — by which the built system forced MAGE out of it, and can name why each rung was safe to climb only because the step below first minted the control that caught what the delegation dropped.
declarations.anchor: The merged chapter: 'What ultimately got built' (six-responsibility tour + system-overview figure), 'The LLM as a function call' (#llm-as-function-call), and 'The staircase' with the five rung lead-ins (Co-coder / QA / Review lead / Tech lead / Architect) + the mage-staircase figure.

declarations.obj: what the method changes for how software engineering is measured, staffed, and taught
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can evaluate the discipline-level implications: where judgment moved, what saturates, and why models are a common language of mature engineering.

declarations.obj: the part of the engineering work that stays the reader's own, and where to take the method next
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can identify the part of the work that stays human and choose where to go next.

declarations.obj: the book within the software-engineering literature — Software Engineering at Google, the Gang of Four, and Model-Driven Software Engineering
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can situate MAGE within the software-engineering literature — mechanized discipline (SE at Google), the design-pattern form (the Gang of Four), and the modeling tradition (MDSE) — as older aspirations under new economics.
declarations.anchor: Section titles 'the-same-two-questions-four-answers', 'standing-on-three-books' (Software Engineering at Google, the Gang of Four, Model-Driven Software Engineering), 'older-aspirations-new-economics', 'placing-mage'.

declarations.obj: six independent industrial systems as evidence for and against MAGE's claims — the modeling ceiling, the convergence buckets, and the gap/orphan diagnosis — without mistaking corroboration for a controlled test
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can analyze six independent industrial systems as evidence for and against MAGE's claims — the modeling ceiling where the software-first sites fall silent, the convergence buckets they share anyway, and the gap/orphan diagnosis read across the six sites — without mistaking corroboration across reconstructions for a controlled test.

declarations.obj: why studying a governed environment demands a new empirical regime — fallible oracles, the limits of per-task ablation, deep single-case evidence, and a fixed intelligence input
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can evaluate why a governed environment demands a new empirical regime: the oracle is itself fallible, per-task ablation cannot price the environment, deep single-case evidence is a legitimate method, and the intelligence input must be held fixed to measure what the environment does.

declarations.obj: the MAGE theory as a causal-loop dynamic model — its constructs, feedback dynamics, hypotheses, propositions, and predictions
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can explain the MAGE theory as a causal-loop dynamic model: its constructs, the four feedback dynamics, the seven hypotheses and two propositions, and the predictions and research agenda they imply.

declarations.obj: a metric one level deeper than the number a decision needs
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can apply Ousterhout's rule and measure one level deeper than the surface number — reading a per-service cost split or a boot-time breakdown as a decision the invoice-level number buried.
declarations.anchor: point: ousterhouts-rule-measure-one-level-deeper / some-evidence-is-mechanically-decidable-other-evidence-is-judgment-laden (4.4 'Measure the State That Matters').

declarations.obj: coverage measured one level deeper — model-claim coverage joined from a traceability graph and the coverage oracle
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can compute coverage measured one level deeper — joining a traceability graph's claim-to-anchor edges with the coverage oracle so the metric counts model claims instead of lines, names an unexercised invariant instead of a percentage, and reports an honest exercised/unmeasurable/out-of-surface breakdown.
declarations.anchor: point: requirements-based-coverage-measures-at-the-semantic-unit (4.4 'One hard example: coverage measured one level deeper').

declarations.obj: a soft, judgment-laden metric that aims a reader and must not be wired to a gate
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can classify a soft metric — a doc-derived test's coverage-of-doc-claims — as one that aims a reader rather than deciding, recognize why its softness is inseparable from a readiness judgment about the seam, and see why wiring it to a blocking gate manufactures hollow tests.

declarations.obj: why a structured model is not a picture of the metric machinery but the machinery itself
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can explain why the MBSE models are consumed at runtime to produce the metrics — the cold-start numbers and the coverage graph both read at check time — so a component-distance grade read from the model drives a pre-commit gate three ways, the model being the machinery rather than a picture of it.

declarations.obj: the semantic gap between a model and the code it governs
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can define the semantic gap — enforcing a property at the wrong level of abstraction — and identify the level where it becomes legible.

declarations.obj: a mechanism on the soft-to-hard spectrum by whether it aims or holds
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can classify a governance mechanism on the soft-to-hard spectrum — guidance that aims versus machinery that holds.
declarations.anchor: point: guidance-aims-enforcement-binds (4.1 the MAGE Workflow, 'Guidance or Enforcement?' — guidance aims, enforcement binds).

declarations.obj: the leap a transformation makes to the model it produces and the guarantee it carries
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can size a transformation's leap to its model and its guarantee.
declarations.anchor: point: size-work-as-transformations-with-checkable-boundaries / docable-sizes-the-leap-to-bounded-typed-edits-the-unit-of-delegation-lines-up-with-a-unit-of-evidence (4.1 'Size Work to Reasoning and Assurance'; sizing-the-leap).

declarations.obj: the core generative-validation move — a generator hunting a counterexample to a model
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can apply the one move behind property testing, fuzzing, and fuzz-MBSE: a generator hunting a counterexample to a stated model.
declarations.anchor: point: let-the-claim-choose-the-search / fix-the-stable-obligation-not-the-seed (4.3 Validating Change, 'Generate Falsifying Evidence' — property / fuzz / TLA+ all hunt a counterexample to a stated model).

declarations.obj: which generative-validation strategy fits a given specification
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can choose which validation strategy to reach for by the specification it attacks.
declarations.anchor: point: let-the-claim-choose-the-search / the-three-cases-make-the-rule-concrete (4.3 'Generate Falsifying Evidence' — the shape of the property chooses the strategy).

declarations.obj: a runbook that gives deterministic steps tools and judgment steps the roughest algorithm that still fits
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can author a runbook that separates deterministic steps from judgment ones — giving the deterministic parts an executable tool that also yields a reusable trace, and the judgment parts a rubric or the roughest algorithm that still fits, up to a pre-canned brief for delegation.

declarations.obj: a lifecycle's healthy path and the failure states off each node, naming the way out and the prohibition
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can map a lifecycle — the healthy path of a recurring activity plus, from each node, its failure states and the action for each — as a failure-mode-and-effects grid, and encode the way out and the prohibition an agent cannot supply on its own.

declarations.obj: the roughest-algorithm rule to a judgment step, reaching for a rubric or a pre-canned brief
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can apply the roughest-algorithm-that-still-fits rule to a judgment step — giving a well-constrained decision an algorithm, an open-ended one only hints, a measurement a rubric, and a delegated task a pre-canned brief.
declarations.anchor: point: type-each-runbook-step-execute-delegate-escalate / surround-a-judgment-step-with-deterministic-work (4.4 'Externalize Operational Judgment' — the roughest-algorithm framing folded into the Execute/Delegate/Escalate step typing).

declarations.obj: the self-governance skill: convert a recurred failure into a durable control
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can use the self-governance signal — a bad thing happened twice — to mint a control instead of re-patching the instance.

declarations.obj: the residual goals no mechanism reaches, why they stay human judgment, and how authoring a spec pulls one out
declarations.statement: After this section, the reader can identify the residual — goals that are neither preventable nor detectable because the failure is an absence nobody specified — explain why it sets the throughput ceiling and is the complement of the two moves rather than a third axis value, and see how authoring the missing spec pulls a goal out of it.

declarations.obj: environmental authority into four roles — a constraint, a sensor, a validator, and a gate — and name the roles bundled inside one artifact
declarations.statement: After this chapter, the reader can decompose environmental authority into four roles — a constraint narrows what can happen, a sensor produces evidence, a validator judges that evidence against an obligation, and a gate controls admission — and name the roles bundled inside one artifact.
